The reproductive biology of the Bastard sole (Microchirus azevia) begins with a broadcast spawning event, during which gamete release occurs in the water column. Following external fertilisation, the fertilised ova develop as pelagic eggs that drift with the currents. At the moment of eclosion, the newly emerged prolarvae are notably small, with a total length at birth of just 0.34 cm [Lb = 0.34 cm] and a corresponding wet weight at birth of 0.000516 g [Wwb = 0.000516 g]. This minute size is characteristic of many flatfishes that produce large numbers of small offspring, reflecting a strategy that prioritises fecundity over individual offspring investment. During the yolk-sac larval stage, these endotrophic larvae rely entirely on their endogenous yolk reserves for sustenance. The yolk absorption stage is a critical period, as the larvae must undergo retinal differentiation and mouth opening before their yolk supply is exhausted to successfully initiate first exogenous feeding. The transition from a pelagic, exogenously feeding larva to a benthic juvenile involves a dramatic larval metamorphosis, during which the body plan undergoes a profound reorganisation, including the migration of one eye to the opposite side of the head, a defining feature of the pleuronectiform body plan.

As the juveniles settle to the seafloor and transition into the benthic juvenile phase, somatic growth proceeds steadily. The wet weight at puberty is reached when individuals attain a body mass of 53.68 g [Wwp = 53.68 g], a value indicative of the sub-adult stage when reproductive structures begin to mature. Concurrently, the total length at puberty measures 17.51 cm [Lp = 17.51 cm], representing the standard length at which the onset of gonadal activity is first detectable through histological examination of the gonads. These morphological milestones are reached after a considerable developmental period. Under the uniform thermal conditions of 13.8 °C [T = 13.8 °C], which represents the ambient water temperature typical of this species' demersal habitat in the northeastern Atlantic, the time since birth at puberty is recorded at 1438.54 days [tp = 1438.54 days]. This protracted juvenile phase is not uncommon among flatfishes that inhabit cool, temperate waters, where slower metabolic rates postpone the onset of reproductive maturity relative to warmer-water congeners.

Towards the culmination of the juvenile growth trajectory, individuals continue to increase in both length and mass until they approach their asymptotic size. The maximum recorded length for this species, or ultimate total length, has been documented at 39.27 cm [Li = 39.27 cm] based on extensive field surveys conducted along the continental shelf. Correspondingly, the ultimate wet weight attained by fully grown adults is approximately 572.7 g [Wwi = approximately 572.7 g], a mass that reflects the species' status as a medium-sized soleid. These asymptotic dimensions are consistent with the general growth pattern observed in other members of the Soleidae, where adult body size is often correlated with the energetic constraints of a low-metabolism, benthic lifestyle. The achievement of this maximum size typically occurs well after the onset of sexual maturity, as the species continues to allocate resources towards somatic growth even during its reproductive years. Field records indicate that the largest specimens are often those that have had access to rich foraging grounds of polychaetes and small crustaceans over many years.

Reproductive output in Microchirus azevia has been characterised through laboratory-based studies of captive gravid individuals. Under the stable thermal regime of 13.8 °C [T = 13.8 °C], which mirrors the bottom temperatures of its native habitat, females exhibit a maximum daily reproductive rate equivalent to a fecundity of approximately 422.79 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 422.79 eggs per day]. This high daily output is partitioned across the spawning season, during which females release multiple batches of pelagic eggs. The repeated spawning events are an example of batch spawning, a common strategy among marine teleosts that allows the species to spread reproductive risk across the season and to take advantage of temporally variable food availability for the larvae. The daily egg production is notable when compared to other flatfishes of similar body size, suggesting a relatively high metabolic investment in gamete production that is sustained by the ample benthic prey resources available in the species' soft-sediment habitat. Such a high fecundity is likely essential for offsetting the elevated mortality rates experienced during the pelagic larval phase.

Longevity in the Bastard sole has been assessed through otolith age readings derived from wild-caught specimens. The data indicate that the maximum recorded lifespan under natural conditions, at the ambient temperature of 13.8 °C [T = 13.8 °C], is 2555.0 days [am = 2555.0 days], which translates to roughly seven years. This lifespan is typical for a medium-sized, temperate flatfish and falls within the range documented for other soleid species such as Solea solea. The age structure of local populations suggests that post-reproductive mortality increases markedly after the sixth year, with very few individuals surviving beyond the eighth year. The natural mortality rate is influenced by predation from larger demersal fish, such as gadoids and elasmobranchs, as well as by the energetic costs of reproduction. The extended juvenile phase, coupled with a moderate adult lifespan, gives Microchirus azevia a relatively slow life-history pace compared to short-lived, fast-growing teleosts, aligning it more closely with the K-selected end of the life-history continuum among its shallow-water flatfish counterparts.
